title: What a Database Is
subtitle: Why you can't just use a file — and what a database actually promises
objectives: Explain what a database gives you that a plain file cannot
Model data with tables, rows, primary keys, and foreign keys, and say why each fact lives in one place
Predict whether a query scans or jumps, and reason about what that costs
Explain durability and concurrency guarantees, and why the database is the hardest thing to scale

lessons.title: Why not just use a file?

exercises.prompt: You store users in users.txt. Two people sign up at the exact same instant and both write to the file. What happens?
choices: Both are saved correctly — the OS handles it
The writes can interleave or overwrite each other, and one signup is silently lost
The file locks itself automatically
The second write is queued perfectly
exercises.why: A plain file has no concurrency control. Two writers can clobber each other, and you lose data with no error at all. Handling concurrent writers safely is one of the main reasons databases exist.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the first thing everyone rediscovers when they 'just use a file.' It works flawlessly with one user and breaks the moment there are two — and the silence is the dangerous part. Nothing crashes, nothing logs. A signup simply never happened.

exercises.prompt: What does a database give you that a plain file does not? Select all.
choices: Safe concurrent access for many readers and writers
Finding one record without reading the whole file
Surviving a crash in the middle of a write
Storing bytes on a disk
exercises.why: Storing bytes is the one thing a file already does perfectly well. Everything else — concurrency, querying, crash safety — is what you're actually buying.
exercises.goDeeper: Worth stating plainly: a database is not 'a fancy file.' It's a concurrency system, a query engine, and a crash-recovery system that happens to keep bytes on a disk. Those three problems are why it's the most complex component you'll run.

exercises.prompt: Your process is killed halfway through writing a record to a file. What state is the file in?
choices: Clean — the OS finishes the write for you
Possibly half-written and corrupt, with no record of what was in progress
It automatically rolls back to the previous version
Completely unchanged
exercises.why: Nothing protects a partial write. You can be left with half a record and no way to know what was meant to happen — corrupt data that looks like real data.
exercises.goDeeper: A database refuses to leave you there. It uses a log of intended changes so that after a crash it can recover to a clean state — either the change fully happened or it fully didn't. You'll see exactly how in this unit's last lesson.

exercises.prompt: users.txt has 10 million lines. You need the user with email x@y.com. What must you do?
choices: Jump directly to that line
Read lines one by one until you find it — up to 10 million reads
Ask the operating system to find it instantly
Nothing — files are searchable by default
exercises.why: A file has no idea what's inside it. Finding anything means scanning everything. A database can jump straight to a record — and that difference is the entire game at scale.
exercises.goDeeper: How it jumps is the subject of the Indexes unit. For now, hold the shape of the problem: 'scan everything' versus 'go straight there' is a difference of a million times, not a few percent.

exercises.prompt: A ______ is a program built to store data safely and let many users query and change it at once.
choices: database
filesystem
cache
compiler
exercises.why: Storage is the least interesting part of the definition. Safety under concurrency and the ability to query are the point.

exercises.prompt: So what's the honest one-sentence reason databases exist?
choices: Disks are hard to write to directly
Because storing data is easy, but querying it, sharing it between many concurrent users, and not losing it in a crash are all hard
They compress data better
They're required by web frameworks
exercises.why: Every feature of a database traces back to one of those three hard problems: find it fast, share it safely, never lose it.
exercises.goDeeper: Keep this frame. When you later evaluate any storage technology — SQL, NoSQL, a cache, object storage — you're really asking which of those three it does well, and which it quietly gives up.

exercises.prompt: You're storing users and their orders. Why put them in two separate tables instead of one big table?
choices: Two tables are always faster
So each fact lives in exactly one place — a user's email is stored once, not repeated on every order
There's no real reason; it's convention
To use less disk space overall
exercises.why: If you repeat a user's email on all 500 of their orders, you now have 500 places to update when it changes — and 500 opportunities for them to disagree with each other.
exercises.goDeeper: This is normalization, and it's the core idea of the relational model: every fact lives in exactly one place. Later you'll learn when to deliberately break this rule (denormalization) to buy speed — but you break it knowingly, accepting the update problem you just re-created.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece of the relational model to what it is.

pairs.right: A collection of rows of the same shape
The agreed shape of the data

exercises.why: Tables hold rows, rows have columns, and the schema is the contract describing what shape every row must take.
exercises.goDeeper: Notice 'schema' is the same idea as an API contract from unit 3 — an agreement about shape that many parties depend on. And it has the same property: changing it once people depend on it is the hard part.

exercises.prompt: What is a primary key?
choices: The first column in the table
A value that uniquely identifies one row — no two rows can share it
The password protecting the table
The largest column
exercises.why: The primary key is a row's identity. It's the handle you use to find, reference, and link that exact row.
exercises.goDeeper: Which is why using an email as a primary key is a trap: everything else about a row can change, but identity shouldn't. People change emails — and now every table that referenced them must change too. Prefer a meaningless, stable id.

exercises.prompt: The orders table has a user_id column pointing at users.id — a foreign key. What does that buy you?
choices: Nothing beyond documentation
It links the order to its user AND lets the database refuse to create an order for a user who doesn't exist
Faster queries only
Automatic encryption of the column
exercises.why: A foreign key is a relationship and a guarantee at once. The database itself refuses to create orphan rows — orders belonging to nobody.
exercises.goDeeper: That's a constraint: a rule the database enforces no matter who writes to it — your API, a migration script, a colleague's one-off query at 2am, an intern with psql. Rules in application code get bypassed by the next writer. Rules in the database cannot be.

exercises.prompt: Why is having a schema useful? Select all.
choices: The database rejects malformed data before it's ever stored
Anyone reading the table knows exactly what to expect
It lets the database store and read the data efficiently
It makes changing the shape of your data effortless
exercises.why: A schema buys you enforcement, shared understanding, and efficient storage. What it emphatically does not buy is easy change — altering a schema on a huge live table is genuinely hard.
exercises.goDeeper: And that last point is the real tradeoff, not a footnote. Schema gives you guarantees today and friction tomorrow. That exact tension is the seed of the SQL vs NoSQL argument you'll meet in the very next unit — it's a debate about when structure is worth its cost.

exercises.prompt: The ______ key uniquely identifies a row; a foreign key points at another table's row.
choices: primary
secondary
index
search
exercises.why: Primary key = this row's identity. Foreign key = a reference to some other row's identity. Together they're how the relational model links data without duplicating it.

lessons.title: How the database finds your data

exercises.prompt: You run: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'x@y.com' — on 10 million rows, with no index on email. What does the database do?
choices: Jumps straight to the matching row
Reads all 10 million rows, checking each one — a full table scan
Asks the operating system to find it
Refuses to run the query
exercises.why: Without an index, the database does exactly what your text file did: reads everything. Writing SQL doesn't make something fast — it just makes it possible.
exercises.goDeeper: Critical mental model: SQL is a request, not a promise about speed. The same query can take 1ms or 10 seconds depending entirely on whether a suitable index exists. People are shocked by this because the query text looks identical either way.

exercises.prompt: Now: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 42, where id is the primary key. Fast or slow?
choices: Slow — same as scanning every row
Fast — the primary key is automatically indexed, so the database jumps straight there
Slow, because it uses the disk
It depends on the table's size, always
exercises.why: Primary keys come with an index for free. That's why looking up by id is instant while looking up by an unindexed email is a scan.
exercises.goDeeper: This is why so many systems feel fine in development. Everyone looks things up by id at first, which is always fast. The scans arrive later — with the features that search by email, by name, by status.

exercises.prompt: Match each concept to what it means.

pairs.right: A question you ask of the data
Reading every row to find matches
Combining rows from two tables via a link
The database's decision about HOW to run your query

exercises.why: You ask a question; the planner decides the strategy; a scan is the brute-force one; a join reassembles data you deliberately split apart.
exercises.goDeeper: Joins are the payoff for normalizing: store each fact once, reassemble views of it on demand. But reassembly isn't free — and joining huge tables is precisely where the relational model starts to hurt at scale. That pain is a major reason NoSQL and denormalization exist.

exercises.prompt: Why is SQL called a 'declarative' language?
choices: Because it's verbose and hard to read
You declare WHAT data you want; the database decides HOW to fetch it
Because you declare variables before using them
It's just a historical name
exercises.why: You describe the result you want. The query planner chooses the strategy — which index to use, which table to read first, how to join.
exercises.goDeeper: This is both a superpower and a landmine. Superpower: the planner has statistics about your data and can optimize better than you'd hand-code. Landmine: a small change in the data distribution can make the planner pick a different plan, and your query falls off a performance cliff with zero code changes. 'Nothing changed, but it got slow' is usually this.

exercises.prompt: A full scan must check 10 million rows. If the database can check roughly 1 million rows per second, about how many seconds does that one query take?
exercises.why: 10 million ÷ 1 million per second = about 10 seconds — for a single query. Now picture 100 users running it at once.
exercises.goDeeper: This is why 'scan vs indexed lookup' isn't a nice-to-have optimization. It's the difference between a product and an outage: those 100 concurrent scans saturate your database, queue up (remember unit 4), and take down every other query too — including the fast ones.

exercises.prompt: Which of these actually make a query faster? Select all.
choices: An index on the column you filter by
Fetching only the columns you actually need
Using SELECT * on a huge table
Filtering in the database instead of in your application code
exercises.why: Index the column you filter on, ask for less data, and let the database do the filtering. SELECT * on a wide table is the opposite — it drags columns you'll never read across the network.
exercises.goDeeper: 'Filter in the database, not in the app' deserves special emphasis: pulling a million rows over the network to filter them down to ten in Python is the single most common performance sin in web development. Move the work to the data — the data is heavy and the answer is light.

exercises.prompt: You INSERT a row and the database returns success. Then the power dies. Is your row there when it comes back up?
choices: No — it was still in memory
Yes — 'success' means the database durably recorded it before answering
Only if it was small
Only if you waited a few seconds
exercises.why: That's the promise, and it's the whole point of the word 'committed': it survives a crash. If commit didn't mean that, it would mean nothing at all.
exercises.goDeeper: The trick is the write-ahead log (WAL). Before touching the real data, the database appends a record of what it's about to do to a sequential log and forces THAT to disk. After a crash it replays the log. That's how you get durability without paying for a slow random disk write on every single change.

exercises.prompt: Why is the write-ahead log fast, even though it forces data onto disk before returning?
choices: It's kept in memory only
It's a sequential append — and appending is dramatically faster than writing randomly across the disk
It's compressed
It isn't fast; it's just a necessary cost
exercises.why: The log is append-only. The disk writes one continuous stream instead of hopping around to update scattered data pages — and sequential beats random by a huge margin.
exercises.goDeeper: Sequential vs random access is one of the largest performance facts in all of storage, and databases are engineered around it rather than pretending disk behaves like RAM. Once you notice it, you see it everywhere: log-structured storage, Kafka, SSD write patterns.

exercises.prompt: Two requests read a counter (value 10), each adds 1 in application code, and each writes back 11. What just happened?
choices: The counter is 12 — correct
The counter is 11 — one increment vanished silently
The database throws an error
The counter stays at 10
exercises.why: This is a lost update. Both read 10, both computed 11, both wrote 11. One user's increment simply disappeared — with no error anywhere.
exercises.goDeeper: It's the users.txt problem again, wearing a database costume. The fix is to stop doing read-modify-write in your app and let the database do it atomically (UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1), or use a transaction with proper isolation — the subject of the Transactions & ACID unit. The lesson that matters right now: concurrency bugs don't crash, they quietly corrupt.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are guarantees the DATABASE should enforce, rather than your application code? Select all.
choices: Uniqueness — no two users with the same email
Referential integrity — no order without a real user
Crash-safe durability of committed data
Business rules like 'premium users get 20% off'
exercises.why: Constraints and durability belong in the database — it enforces them for every writer, forever. Business policy doesn't: it changes with the product and belongs in the app.
exercises.goDeeper: The test: 'would this rule still be true no matter which app, script, or human writes to this table?' If yes, it's a data invariant — put it in the database where it can't be bypassed. If it's policy that marketing might change next quarter, keep it in the application.

exercises.prompt: Your signup code checks 'does this email already exist?' and then INSERTs if not. Two signups for the same email race each other. What breaks?
choices: Nothing — the check handles it
Both checks pass before either insert runs, so you get two users with the same email
The database deadlocks
The second request is automatically rejected
exercises.why: Check-then-act is a race, always. Between your check and your insert, the other request slips through — and both believe they're the first.
exercises.goDeeper: The only reliable fix is a UNIQUE constraint in the database, letting one insert fail and handling that error. This is why the database is the last line of defense: it's the single point every writer must pass through. Application checks are advisory; database constraints are law.

exercises.prompt: You're recording analytics events at enormous volume — billions per day. Slide toward how strictly each write must be durable.
exercises.rightLabel: Batched / fire-and-forget (fast, may lose a few)
exercises.why: Losing a handful of events out of billions changes no decision anyone will ever make. Throughput matters vastly more here than perfect durability — so batch hard and accept a little loss.
exercises.goDeeper: This is unit 5's 'what does it cost to be wrong?' applied to durability. Not all data deserves the same promises: a payment must never vanish; an analytics ping can. Paying for guarantees you don't need is exactly how you build a system that's slow AND expensive.

exercises.prompt: Why is the database usually the hardest part of a system to scale?
choices: It's written in a low-level language
It's the stateful source of truth — app servers are disposable clones, but copies of data must agree with each other
Because it uses a disk
Because the software is old
exercises.why: Your app servers are interchangeable and you scale them by adding boxes. The database holds the truth — and the moment you want a second copy of the truth for scale, you inherit replication, consistency, and conflict.
exercises.goDeeper: This is unit 5's lens at its sharpest. You deliberately concentrated your state here, which makes the database simultaneously your most valuable component and your bottleneck. Everything ahead — indexes, replication, sharding, CAP, consistency models — is a consequence of that one decision.
